sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Increasing impact of traffic on transportation and traffic management systems has become a critical concern for urban 
planning. As cities grow and populations rise, the demand for efficient transportation systems and effective traffic man-
agement strategies has intensified. Congestion is a significant consequence of increasing traffic, leading to longer travel 
times, reduced fuel efficiency, higher pollution, and greater risks of accidents and fatalities.
Traditional traffic prediction methodologies, such as statistical models, often struggle to effectively capture the intri-
cate and dynamic nature of real-time traffic patterns. In contrast, deep learning architectures, particularly hybrid mod-
els, offer substantial enhancements in this domain. The Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM model integrates convolutional neural 
networks (CNNs), gated recurrent units (GRUs), and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to adeptly manage the

spatial–temporal complexities inherent in traffic data. This integration enables the model to proficiently extract spa -
tial features through CNNs, model temporal dependencies via GRUs, and retain long-term temporal information using 
LSTMs, thereby improving the accuracy and robustness of traffic flow predictions. For instance, a study demonstrated 
that a hybrid CNN-GRU model outperformed traditional methods in traffic flow forecasting by effectively capturing both 
spatial and temporal dependencies.
CNNs capture spatial relationships between road segments, identifying how vehicle flow is interconnected across 
different areas. GRU and LSTM layers model the temporal aspects, learning from historical data to predict future traffic 
conditions at road junction based on short-term fluctuations and long-term trends. This hybrid model ensures a more 
accurate prediction of traffic flow than traditional models, which typically struggle with the dynamic and multi-layered 
nature of traffic.
By leveraging the power of deep learning, Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM enables more reliable real-time traffic predictions, 
allowing for better congestion management, enhanced road safety, and more efficient urban transportation systems. 
This predictive accuracy not only improves daily traffic flow but also aids long-term infrastructure planning, helping cities 
meet the growing demands of urbanization.
Efficient traffic management depends on minimizing traveller waiting times at junctions and optimizing their flow 
through the road network. Traffic prediction at junction forecasts vehicle movement at specific intersections to estimate 
the number of vehicles, their movements, and traffic timing. Advanced technologies and data analysis techniques, such 
as historical data analysis, sensor and camera networks, and machine learning models, are employed to achieve accurate 
predictions. Deep learning models such as the dynamic graph convolution neural network [1 ] and geometric feature 
extraction based on the dynamic convolutional neural network [2 ] have been adopted to address varied engineering 
problems. In this context, deep learning is also gaining attention for smart city solutions, and a recent survey [3] explores 
its applications, progress, challenges, and opportunities to inspire experts and new researchers in the field.
These solutions promote and enhance public transportation networks, encouraging the use of mass transit and 
reducing the reliance on private vehicles. Additionally, promoting the expansion of road infrastructure and alternative 
transportation modes, such as cycling and walking, can help alleviate traffic congestion. However, these solutions can 
only be implemented with a major breakthrough in the regulatory mechanisms and a change in the mindset of people 
at large. Until such a change happens, it is evident that an effective traffic management system must be developed and 
implemented to tackle the issues caused by rising traffic congestion.
The modern city is transforming into an intelligent city as urbanization and population expansion imposes signifi -
cant challenges on urban traffic control. An Intelligent Transportation System (ITS) employs advanced technologies to 
enhance traffic management. It accomplishes this by utilizing real-time monitoring, adjusting traffic signals dynamically, 
and providing adaptive route guidance. An ITS is a crucial element of a well-planned smart city, with the prediction of 
traffic on a particular road as a crucial ITS constituent. Precise traffic prediction plays a vital role in a wide range of real-
life scenarios, including reducing congestion and enabling vehicle demand prediction. The continuously increasing 
availability of traffic-related data offers exciting opportunities to investigate this problem from additional perspectives.
Researchers use intelligent transportation approaches to estimate traffic flow using statistical models, which involves 
substantial work owing to established assumptions that may result in inaccurate predictions. Deep neural models such 
as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) may enhance prediction accuracy by remembering past data. However, because of 
the vanishing gradient problem, RNNs may lose the memory of more extensive sequences over time [2]. Researchers have 
suggested numerous RNN modifications to overcome this problem. LSTM and GRU are commonly employed. The GRU 
model, first introduced by [3], tries to avoid the frequent vanishing gradient issue in traditional recurrent neural networks.
In this research, we focus on predicting traffic flow. A deep learning model is presented that combines a hybrid archi-
tecture of CNN, GRU, and LSTM to forecast the number of vehicles passing through a particular junction, as illustrated 
in Fig. 1. The study sheds light on the hybridization of these three techniques, presenting the Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM 
model and showcasing its efficacy in traffic flow prediction tasks. Furthermore, the research provides an overview of traf-
fic prediction at junctions and explores the implications of increasing traffic on transportation and traffic management 
systems. Integrating CNN, GRU, and LSTM architectures into a hybrid deep learning model can effectively capture the 
spatial and temporal dynamics of traffic flow, leading to significantly improved traffic prediction accuracy compared to 
state-of-the-art methods.
The research begins with exploring the dataset, followed by data pre-processing and feature engineering to prepare 
the data for training, subsequent to which the models are applied. The main contributions of our research work are as 
follows:

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.text:
Traditional traffic prediction methods, such as statistical models (e.g., ARIMA) and time-series forecasting, fall short of 
capturing the complex, non-linear, and high-dimensional nature of real-world traffic data. These methods struggle to 
model both spatial and temporal dependencies, limiting their accuracy and generalization across different traffic condi-
tions. In contrast, deep learning and hybrid models, like Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM, offer superior performance by effectively 
handling the spatial–temporal interactions within traffic data. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) extract spatial 
features, while GRU and LSTM layers capture short-term and long-term temporal dependencies, respectively. This inte -
gration improves the model’s capacity to capture complex patterns, adapt to dynamic conditions, and support real-time 
applications in intelligent transportation systems. With access to large datasets and the ability to continuously learn from 
streaming data, deep learning models provide more accurate, flexible, and scalable traffic predictions, outperforming 
traditional methods in modern traffic control and management systems. Below, we discuss the related work based on 
these approaches and explain why we chose hybridization to improve prediction performance.

2.1  Traditional machine learning and statistical approaches for traffic prediction
Traffic prediction is critical in traffic management systems because it may assist in optimizing resource utilization, mini-
mizing congestion, and improving safety. Recent studies on traffic prediction utilizing deep learning techniques have 
been undertaken. Several recent surveys have examined traffic prediction literature from various perspectives in spe -
cific contexts. A survey conducted between 2004 and 2013 reviewed various methods and applications and identified 
significant challenges during that time period. It primarily focuses on short-term traffic prediction and relies mainly on 
traditional methods [4]. Another research [5] also prioritized short-term traffic prediction and provided an overview of 
prediction techniques and research recommendations. In addition, the paper [6 ] supplied information on obtaining 
road traffic data. To estimate traffic congestion, a predictive model was presented that used real-time data from a traf-
fic monitoring system and multiple machine learning techniques [ 7], such as Gradient Boosting (GB), Support Vector 
Machine (SVM), and Random Forest (RF). The authors evaluate the performance of the suggested system by comparing 
the prediction accuracy of the different machine-learning algorithms.
Predicting traffic congestion levels using Extreme Learning Machines (ELMs), which can learn from new data on 
the fly without retraining the entire model, has been investigated [8 ]. This method is compared with other traditional 
approaches, demonstrating that the proposed model outperforms them in terms of prediction accuracy. The authors 
also experimented with different hyperparameters to optimize the model’s performance.
Traditional approaches to traffic prediction comprise statistical techniques. The statistical process involves develop -
ing a model from data for making predictions, utilizing machine learning models ARIMA [9 ], and VAR [10]. However, 
these methods have specific requirements for traffic data, which can take time to meet when dealing with complex and 
dynamic traffic data. Additionally, these traditional methods are used to evaluate and analysis small datasets. Several 
conventional machine learning methods like Support Vector Regression [11] and Random Forest Regression [12] have 
been suggested for traffic prediction to address these limitations.
2.2  Deep learning application in traffic flow prediction
LSTM and GRU are advanced deep learning models designed to handle sequence-based prediction tasks, such as traf-
fic flow forecasting [13]. Both LSTM and GRU are specialized recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that capture long-term 
dependencies in time-series data, making them highly effective for predicting future traffic patterns based on historical 
data. LSTMs use a memory cell controlled by three gates—input, output, and forget gates—that regulate the flow of 
information, enabling the model to retain or discard information as needed. This structure allows LSTMs to overcome 
the vanishing gradient problem in traditional RNNs, making them particularly useful for capturing long-term patterns 
in traffic data, such as recurring congestion during rush hours or seasonal fluctuations.
GRUs, on the other hand, are a simpler alternative to LSTMs. They combine the input and forget gates into a unified 
‘update gate’ , reducing the complexity of the model while maintaining similar performance. GRUs are computationally 
more efficient than LSTMs and often perform comparably, especially in tasks where shorter-term dependencies are more 
prominent. In traffic prediction, both LSTM and GRU excel at learning the temporal dynamics of vehicle flow, allowing 
them to make highly accurate forecasts. These models have demonstrated significant improvements in traffic prediction 
accuracy compared to traditional time-series methods, leading to better real-time traffic management, reduced conges-
tion, and improved long-term urban planning. Their ability to process both immediate variations and extended trends 
makes them ideal for solving complex transportation problems.
Meanwhile, [14] provided a comprehensive survey of traffic prediction using machine learning techniques, including at 
intersections. The authors discussed the different approaches used to process traffic data and highlighted the strengths 
and weaknesses of each approach. The traffic flow prediction model introduced in [15] utilizes graph convolutional 
neural networks to enhance intersection traffic control. By employing actual traffic data from real-world scenarios, they 
substantiated the efficiency of their model. This research expands in [16] to propose a traffic flow prediction model that 
uses deep learning with an attention mechanism to improve intersection control.
A short-term algorithm for traffic flow prediction improves junction management by combining deep learning with 
spatial and temporal data. Their approach considers geographical and temporal correlations in traffic data, resulting in 
more accurate forecasts. Meanwhile, [17] suggested a short-term traffic flow prediction model that improves intersec -
tion management using a convolutional neural network using spatial and temporal information. They tested the model’s 
efficiency by using traffic data from real-world circumstances.

sections.title: 2.5 Traffic prediction using graph neural network
sections.text:
In the context of smart cities, predicting traffic flow remains a important challenge due to the complex interplay of spatio-
temporal factors and non-linear dynamics. Traditional approaches often struggle with high computational costs and fail 
to effectively identify patterns, particularly overlooking relationships between far-apart roads. In contrast, the graph con-
volutional network (GCN) [31] proves to be better suited for handling graph-structured data, like the architecture of traffic 
networks.
The authors in [32] tackle the challenges associated with traffic flow networks by proposing innovative methods. One 
notable approach involves the use of 3D temporal graph convolutional networks (3D-TGCN) for traffic prediction. By con-
structing road graphs based on time series similarity, the need for spatial information becomes redundant. The model’s 
unique 3D graph convolution technique significantly improves accuracy, outperforming existing baseline models in empirical 
evaluations. Likewise, traffic forecasting faces difficulties in capturing intricate spatio-temporal relationships and non-linear 
patterns. Many current methods fail to directly integrate spatio-temporal dependencies, instead handling them separately.
The adaptive graph spatial–temporal transformer network (ASTTN) represents a significant advancement inspired by the 
success of transformer architectures. By leveraging local multi-head self-attention mechanisms on an adaptive spatial–tem-
poral graph, ASTTN effectively captures cross-spatial–temporal correlations and delivers outstanding empirical results [33]. 
Real-world traffic prediction remains challenging due to the dynamic nature of spatiotemporal dependencies in traffic 
data. To address this, the adaptive spatio-temporal convolutional network (ASTCN) is proposed, integrating a spatial graph 
learning module and an adaptive temporal convolution module. Comprehensive experiments on real-world traffic datasets 
demonstrate that ASTCN consistently surpasses state-of-the-art approaches [34].
The complexity of spatial–temporal correlations within road networks further complicates traffic forecasting. The Dual-
Graph framework mitigates this issue by simultaneously modelling traffic dynamics for both nodes and edges, with evalua-
tions on public datasets highlighting its effectiveness, particularly in long-term forecasting scenarios [35]. In fields like trans-
portation and neurology, spatiotemporal forecasting becomes even more complex due to non-linearity, dynamic behaviour, 
and varying road conditions. To overcome these challenges. Dynamic temporal position observant graph neural network 
(DTPO-GNN) is formally presented as a novel architecture. This model incorporates positional awareness and spatial–temporal 
dependencies in traffic flow, using a controlled sample encoder-decoder architecture and two-way random walks. DTPO-GNN 
proves to be an efficient and accurate solution for large-scale road network traffic prediction [36].
The traffic graph convolutional recurrent neural network (T-GCRNN), proposed in [37], addresses large-scale traffic pre-
diction by combining graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) to capture spatial relationships and recurrent neural 
networks (RNNs) to model temporal patterns in traffic data. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that 
T-GCRNN achieves superior performance, especially for long-term traffic forecasting. Similarly, the GCN-DHSTNet model 
effectively forecasts crowd flows, a task complicated by spatial–temporal dependencies and external influences such as 
weather conditions and the distribution of points of interest (POI). By integrating GCN with LSTM networks, GCN-DHSTNet 
leverages multiple temporal granularities and external features to deliver enhanced predictive accuracy [38].
Building on the importance of graph topology, advances in skeleton-based action recognition have led to the develop-
ment of the ACC-GCN model, which introduces attentive channel-wise correlation graph convolution (ACC-GC). This method 
improves graph learning by capturing detailed topological relationships at the channel level, thereby enhancing correlation 
accuracy. The model achieves competitive benchmark results while reducing computational overhead [39].
To address the dynamic and complex spatio-temporal relationships in traffic forecasting, the dynamic multi-fusion graph 
network (DMFGNet) introduces an innovative strategy for dynamically capturing these correlations. Its core component, the 
spatio-temporal attention unit (STAU), optimizes neighbour aggregation weights to improve spatiotemporal integration. 
Validated on real-world datasets within a hybrid edge-cloud infrastructure, DMFGNet delivers exceptional performance, 
reduced latency, and efficient resource usage, highlighting the versatility and effectiveness of graph-based models across 
various applications [39].

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.text:
This research applied advanced deep-learning models to predict traffic flow at intersections. To tackle the complexi-
ties of traffic forecasting, we utilized well-established models such as gated recurrent units (GRU) [40], long short-term 
memory (LSTM) networks [41], and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) [42]. These models were chosen for their 
Vol.:(0123456789)
Discover Computing           (2025) 28:38  | https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-025-09526-0 
 
 Research
effectiveness in capturing the temporal and spatial dynamics critical for traffic prediction. Given the spatiotemporal 
nature of traffic data, we experimented with various combinations, including LSTM-CNN, GRU-LSTM, and CNN-GRU. 
Our experiments revealed that the proposed Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM model achieved the highest accuracy.
The Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM model combines the strengths of CNN for spatial feature extraction and GRU-LSTM 
layers for modelling temporal dependencies. CNN efficiently captures the spatial correlations between road seg-
ments by analyzing vehicle flow patterns in adjacent areas, while the GRU and LSTM layers collaboratively learn 
both short-term fluctuations and long-term trends in traffic flow data. This hybrid approach is essential for accurate 
traffic forecasting, where both spatial proximity and temporal dynamics are crucial. We evaluated the performance 
of Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM across multiple datasets, including the PeMS dataset, England dataset, P/Castellano data-
set, and Fedesoriano dataset. These datasets represent diverse traffic conditions, from urban roads to highways, 
enabling comprehensive testing of the model across different scenarios. The proposed model outperformed other 
combinations in terms of key metrics such as RMSE, MAE, and MAPE. The lower values of these metrics for Hybrid 
CNN-GRU-LSTM signify better predictive accuracy compared to existing models and combinations.
To assess the effectiveness of each model, we carefully performed data acquisition, preprocessing, feature engi-
neering, model training, and evaluation. During the model assessment phase, we applied the aforementioned metrics 
to quantify the prediction accuracy. The results consistently showed that Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM produced superior 
outcomes in terms of both short-term and long-term traffic flow forecasts.
Once trained and tested, the model was deployed in a production environment to predict future traffic conditions. 
The model’s ability to handle large datasets and complex spatial–temporal patterns makes it an invaluable tool for 
real-time traffic management. Figure  2 illustrates the detailed architecture of Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM, demonstrating 
how the CNN layer captures spatial dependencies and how GRU-LSTM layers jointly model temporal dependencies. 
Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM provides a robust solution for traffic prediction by integrating the advantages of CNN, GRU, 
and LSTM into a unified framework. Its application to various datasets showcases its adaptability and accuracy, sig-
nificantly improving upon the predictive capabilities of existing models. The results from our experiments validate 
that Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM offers a reliable and effective approach to mitigating traffic congestion and enhancing 
transportation systems.

3.1  Hybrid CNN‑GRU‑LSTM architecture
The proposed methodology introduces a Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM architecture, as depicted in Fig. 2. This integrated model 
combines CNN, GRU, and LSTM layers to effectively capture both spatial and temporal dependencies inherent in traffic 
data, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy. The model’s hyperparameters are detailed in Table 1. The architecture initi-
ates with a 1D Convolutional Layer utilizing 32 filters with a kernel size of 3, performing one-dimensional convolution 
on the input data. The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function is employed to introduce non-linearity, facilitating 
the extraction of spatial features from the data.
The CNN-GRU-LSTM hybrid model outperforms individual architectures due to its ability to combine the strengths of 
its components. The CNN layer is highly effective at extracting spatial features and identifying localized patterns, such 
as sudden variations or correlations within traffic sequences. The GRU and LSTM layers handle temporal dependencies, 
with GRU efficiently capturing short-term trends and LSTM excelling at learning long-term dependencies through its 
advanced gating mechanisms. This integration allows the model to represent both immediate and extended temporal 
contexts, improving its ability to capture periodic trends and sudden changes. Moreover, the hybrid structure reduces 
the risk of overfitting by balancing the simplicity of GRU with the robustness of LSTM. This comprehensive approach 
results in higher accuracy and better performance compared to standalone CNN-LSTM or GRU-LSTM models, making it 
particularly effective for complex predictive tasks.
In addition to its advantages, the model holds significant potential for practical applications in real-world traffic 
management, particularly in traffic signal control. By accurately predicting traffic flow at specific junctions, the model 
enables dynamic adjustments to signal timings based on anticipated congestion. This real-time adaptability optimizes 
traffic flow, reduces delays, and enhances overall traffic efficiency. Such capabilities are essential for the development 
of smart traffic systems, where data-driven decision-making can lead to more responsive and effective transportation 
networks. Through these practical applications, the model bridges the gap between theoretical potential and real-world 
use, contributing to smarter and more efficient urban traffic management.
Subsequent to the Conv1D layer, a MaxPooling1D layer is incorporated to reduce data dimensionality. Operating with 
a pool size of 2, this layer identifies and extracts the most significant features from the preceding convolutional layer. This 
sequential integration of Conv1D and MaxPooling1D layers optimally contributes to the model’s ability to discern spatial 
intricacies and prioritize essential information, thereby bolstering its efficacy in making accurate predictions within the 
context of traffic data analysis. A Dropout layer with a dropout rate of 0.5 is used to reduce overfitting. Subsequently, 
two Dense layers are added, with the first one having 100 units and ReLU activation. The final Dense layer with one unit 
is utilized for the output prediction.

3.2  GRU‑LSTM and CNN‑LSTM architecture
The GRU-LSTM model is implemented using the TensorFlow library with Keras as the high-level API. GRU-LSTM model 
represent in Fig. 3, model architecture starts with a GRU layer, which processes sequential data and captures temporal 
dependencies effectively. The GRU layer is followed by a dropout layer to prevent overfitting during training. The dropout 
layer helps in regularization and improves the model’s generalization ability. Also, we include an LSTM layer, which further 
refines the sequential information and considers long-term dependencies within the traffic data. The LSTM layer also 
helps in mitigating the vanishing gradient problem, which can occur in deep neural networks during backpropagation. 
A dense layer with a single output unit is added to complete the model architecture, enabling the model to predict the 
number of vehicles as a regression task. The model is trained using the mean squared error loss function and the Adam 
optimizer, which efficiently updates the model’s weights during training.
We implement an early stopping mechanism with a minimum delta of 0.001 and a patience of 100 epochs to prevent

sections.title: 4 Dataset description
sections.text:
This research employs multiple publicly available traffic datasets within our proposed Hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM approach. 
These datasets encompass diverse features and attributes, contributing to the comprehensive analysis conducted in 
this research.

sections.title: 4.1 England dataset
sections.text:
The analysis of the traffic dataset of England is gathered from the Highways England Site [43], capturing traffic flow 
dynamics from January 2020 to November 2020. To explain traffic patterns, particular emphasis is placed on peak hours 
occurring on weekdays, specifically from 8 to 9 AM. This dataset comprises a comprehensive set of observations spanning 
204 days. The dataset contains the parameters like Day Type ID, Carriageway flow, Speed Value and the type of vehicle 
variant in size for every 15 min interval. Figure  5 represents the aggregated values in a day for each parameter. Before 
employing time series forecasting models, the dataset undergoes preprocessing procedures, including normalization 
through the Z-Score Normalization technique. This normalization step is crucial for ensuring the data is appropriately 
standardized, facilitating effective analysis and modeling processes.

sections.title: 4.2 PeMS dataset
sections.text:
Real traffic data was sourced from the Caltrans via the PeMS [44] platform, a traffic monitoring system that provides data 
from California’s road network. The dataset includes traffic flow, mean speed, and traffic density measurements obtained 
from the I5 freeway, chosen due to its extensive coverage and numerous traffic detectors. Three sections of the I5 free -
way were selected, with traffic data collected at 5-minute intervals for 2015 and 2016, totaling 600,000 samples. PeMS

sections.title: 4.3 P/Castellana dataset
sections.text:
In this dataset [45], we identify the predictor variables and the target variable while also specifying the data sources 
utilized for our analyses. The target variable represents the hourly count of vehicles passing through a designated traffic 
station in a specific direction. To evaluate our model, we selected four key traffic stations in Madrid, each representing 
areas with notable traffic volumes and unique features. Among these stations, three are situated in the city’s core districts, 
serving as key nodes in the urban traffic network. Additionally, we included one station located at a major entry/exit 
point of the city. Specifically, Paseo de la Castellana, one of our selected stations, gathers data in the North–South direc-
tion, serving as a significant thoroughfare traversing Madrid from its downtown area towards the North. As a predictor 
variable, we have also considered the hour in the timestep. For each prediction, the input data is offered in four different 
hours, which is aggregated day-wise, as shown in Fig. 7.

sections.title: 4.4 Fedesoriano dataset
sections.text:
The dataset [46] contains date-time information and vehicle count data at a traffic junction. The data spans from Novem-
ber 1, 2015, to June 30, 2016. To improve the data, additional time-based features were derived, including year, month, 
day, hour, and day of the week. These temporal features are subsequently employed for visual analysis, exploring the 
relationships between time components and the ’Vehicles’ variable. Figure  8 presents visualizations with time-related 
features on the x-axis (e.g., year, month), while the ’Vehicles’ count is plotted on the y-axis. Different lines or colors rep -
resent distinct ’Junction’ values. These plots facilitate the identification of temporal patterns in vehicle counts at various 
junctions, providing insights into trends and variations in traffic flow across different times and days. The data collected 
through traffic sensors supports a detailed analysis of traffic patterns, offering a deeper understanding of vehicle move-
ment dynamics at different times of day and week.
After preprocessing, the dataset is divided into training, validation, and testing subsets. The hybrid CNN-GRU-LSTM 
model is trained on the training set, optimized with the validation set to adjust hyperparameters, and evaluated using 
the testing set to measure its performance.

Every intersection of the junction has been seeing a general increasing trend over the last year. As we have established 
before, the fourth junction only contains a small amount of data, and that data would not go back more than a year. 
During the month of June, there is a noticeable increase in traffic at the first and second crossroads. Our presumption 
is that this is because of the summer holidays and the activities that surround them. Monthly, there is a decent consist -
ency in all the data over all dates. We can observe that activity is at its highest throughout the peak working hours of 
the day and that it drops down significantly during the night time hours. This is in line with what was anticipated. When 
considering weekly trends, Sundays often have less congestion than other days of the week since fewer automobiles, 
buses and bikes are on the road. However, the volume of traffic is rather constant throughout the weekdays. In this 
research paper, we observed an upward trend in the yearly data for all four junctions, as mentioned earlier, the first and 
second junctions experienced an arrival of traffic around June, which could be attributed to summer break and related 
activities. Additionally, we found a consistent pattern in the data on a monthly basis, regardless of the date. Daily, traffic 
peaks occur during morning and evening hours, followed by a decline during the night, which is consistent with our 
expectations. Finally, we analyzed the weekly traffic patterns and found that Sundays experience smoother traffic with 
fewer vehicles on the road, while traffic remains steady from Monday to Friday.

sections.title: 5 Experimental setup
sections.text:
The proposed traffic prediction models run on a Windows operating system, which is configured with a Core i5 processor 
and 16 GB of primary memory.
5.1  Performance and parameter
To assess the effectiveness of our proposed hybrid model, we calculate RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and MSE. RMSE is a metric 
for quantifying the disparity between actual and predicted traffic congestion. Equation (5 ) is applied to evaluate RMSE, 
continuously measuring error rates. Additionally, MAE and MAPE are computed using Eqs. (6 ) and (7), respectively, elu-
cidating the model’s predictive accuracy. Furthermore, MSE is calculated using Eq. (8), providing insight into the average 
squared differences between predicted and actual values.
5.2  Hybrid CNN‑GRU‑LSTM algorithm
To instantiate this hybrid model, the Python programming language is connected, in conjunction with the Colab note -
book, to create an integrated development environment. Keras and TensorFlow, as deep learning libraries, are imported 
to facilitate the formulation of an artificial neural network. The architecture of this neural network is characterized by 
three distinct layers.
Firstly, the input layer serves as the initial entry point for the model, accommodating the traffic data alongside their 
associated dates, which correspond to the number of vehicles recorded. Subsequently, the model employs a CNN layer, 
designed to extract spatial features from the input data. This layer serves as a pivotal component in spatial feature
